plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Literacy and Language, Years 5 and 6: responding to an opposing view and writing a conclusion that restates the position, sums up the reasons and calls the reader to act
plan.shape: mine, ours, yours a third time: compare two endings, watch the zoo letter answer back and finish, practise both moves, finish the class shade letter together, then finish their own piece
plan.criticalFeature: a conclusion ends with one clear thing the reader can do now; answering back gives proof, not insults
decisionPoints: the Answer back round (proof after However, not insults)
the choice check: the strongest call to action
the exit board: a call to action written for a new conclusion
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. The ending sells: answer back, restate, sum up, call to action.
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 2? Write the answer back and conclusion today with the frames, then add one body paragraph using the Session 2 Supported Worksheet.

studentTools: Big piece plan and the draft so far (writing books)
Writing books (draft on every second line)
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: The class shade letter so far: introduction, body 1 and body 2
Answer back: Some people say... However...
Conclusion: 1 restate (echo the hook), 2 sum up, 3 call to action

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Short warm-up on the parts of an ending, then plan the answer back and conclusion. The writing goes in writing books.
resources.title: Answer Back and Finish Strong

sections.title: Warm-up: which part of the ending?

example.prompt: 'Please fix our broken path by June.'
steps: Does it tell the reader to do something?
Does it say when?
Then it is the call to action.

items.prompt: Label each sentence: other side, restate, sum up or call to action.
rows: Please build the dog park fence before the summer holidays.
Our town's dogs deserve a safe place to run.
Some people say a fence costs too much.
A fence keeps dogs off the road and, most importantly, keeps kids safe.
answers: Please build the dog park fence before the summer holidays.
Our town's dogs deserve a safe place to run.
Some people say a fence costs too much.
A fence keeps dogs off the road and, most importantly, keeps kids safe.

example.prompt: Other side: 'Zoos teach kids about bears.'
steps: Say their point fairly: Some people say...
Turn it with However.
Give proof, not an insult.
example.answer: However, cameras let kids watch wild bears.

items.prompt: Mia answered the other side like this. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Some people say zoos keep bears safe. They are wrong and silly.
items.answer: It insults the other side and gives no proof. Fix: However, wild bears are safest in protected Arctic habitat, not behind walls.

items.prompt: A letter to the principal about a longer lunch. Which call to action is strongest?
options: Please add ten minutes to lunch from next term.
items.explain: It asks for one clear action and says when.

steps: Answer back: Some people say... However...
Restate: echo your hook.
Sum up your two reasons, then ask: Please...
example.answer: Cameras answer the other side. Twenty steps is no life. Space and cold. Please stop new bears from this year.

items.prompt: Plan each part in a few words. Then write them in your writing book, every second line.
answers: the other side's best point, said fairly
a fact or example that answers it
the position again, using words from the hook
one clear action the reader can take, and when

resources.tip: Finished? Read your whole piece aloud to a partner, then grab the Extension.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: three styles of last line, then read the whole piece as your reader and improve the weakest sentence.
resources.title: Extension: Ending Moves
resources.subtitle: Leave the reader ready to act.

example.prompt: The zoo letter, three last lines
steps: Echo the hook: Give them back their hundreds of kilometres.
Final question: Would you choose twenty steps?
Picture the future: Imagine bears roaming free again.
example.answer: Pick the one your reader will remember.

items.prompt: Write three different last lines for your own piece. Star the best.
answers: repeats or twists words from the opening hook
a rhetorical question the reader answers in their head
shows what happens if the reader acts

example.prompt: The zoo director reads the letter.
steps: Read every paragraph as the reader.
Find the sentence they could argue with most.
Add proof or change a word to fix it.
example.answer: Weak: Zoos are bad. Better: Zoos cannot give bears the space they need.

items.prompt: Read your whole piece as your reader. Copy your weakest sentence, rewrite it, and explain why the new one is harder to argue with.
items.answer: A weak sentence copied, a stronger rewrite with proof or a surer claim, and a reason linked to the reader.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Supported option: circle the part, then an answer back and conclusion frame with a starter for every line.
resources.title: Ending Helper
resources.subtitle: Answer back, then finish strong.

steps: Does it ask the reader to do something?
Yes, it says Please.
So it is the call to action.

items.prompt: Please open the gym on wet days.
Our school needs a gym we can use.
items.hint: Does it say the position again?

items.prompt: Please add bike racks this term.

steps: Some people say zoos teach kids.
However, cameras can too.
Please stop bringing in new bears from this year.
example.answer: Other side, my answer, my ask.

items.prompt: Finish each starter. Then copy your ending into your writing book.
items.hint: Use the other side and the call to action from your plan.

slides.notes: Open the session: today the piece gets its ending, so by the end everyone has a full draft.
Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for students who need it. Keep the class shade letter from Sessions 1 and 2 on the board.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to answer the other side and finish with a strong call to action.
successCriteria: I can name the three parts of a conclusion.
I can write an answer-back paragraph and a conclusion with a clear call to action.
I can make my last line echo my hook.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: You've told your reader what you want and proved it. Today you finish it.
SAY: Let's read the I can lines together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
SAY: Naming the three parts is where everyone starts.
Writing the answer back and the conclusion is today's big goal.
notes.prep: SC1 naming the parts is reachable for all; SC2 answer back plus conclusion is the core; SC3 echoing the hook is the stretch.

slides.title: Which ending would the director remember?

visual.text:
A: That is all. Thanks for reading my letter.
B: Twenty steps a day is no life. Please stop bringing in new bears from this year.

slides.prompt: Which one would make the director act?

notes.answer: B - it echoes the hook and asks for one clear action
beats: SAY: Here are two ways my zoo letter could end.
Read both in your head, and think like the zoo director.
ASK: Which ending would the director remember?
10 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to B
ASK: Why does B work better? Tell your partner.
20 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 20 seconds. Go.
Eyes back in 3, 2, 1.
EXPECT: it reminds you of the start and tells you what to do
SAY: That's it. B echoes my hook, and it asks for something.
Today you write an ending like that, plus an answer to the other side.
trap: choosing A because it is polite.
Fix: ask what does A want the director to do? Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Bridges the hook from Session 1 to today's echo. Week 1's other-side thinking returns in the answer back. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: One clear thing you want the reader to do now.
slides.example: Please switch off one light tonight.

notes.answer: one clear thing the reader can do now
beats: POINT to the words. SAY: These words are call to action. Say them with me.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
SAY: A call to action is like a target.
It tells the reader exactly what to do, and the best ones say when.
ASK: Could your reader actually do the example tonight?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up
trap: a call to action that is a wish, like I hope things change.
Fix: student starts with Please and names one action.
notes.prep: The target picture: one clear thing, aimed at one reader.

slides.title: Mine: watch me answer back
slides.extract: Some people say zoos help children learn to love polar bears. However, wildlife cameras and documentaries let millions of children watch wild bears without taking a single bear from the ice. Learning about bears should never cost a bear its freedom.
highlights: without taking a single bear from the ice
slides.source: Model letter, written for this session

beats: POINT to Some people say.
SAY: First I say the other side's best point, and I say it fairly.
If I make it sound silly, my reader stops trusting me.
POINT to However.
SAY: Then one word turns it back to my side. After it, I give proof.
ASK: Which word turns this paragraph back to my side?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: However
POINT to the last sentence.
SAY: And I finish by selling it, so the director feels the cost.
trap: answering back with an insult, like They are wrong.
Fix: student replaces it with a fact or example after However.
notes.stretch: What else might the other side say, and how would you answer it?
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: Some people say... However...
notes.prep: Mine: the zoo letter's answer-back paragraph. Critical feature: proof after However, never an insult.

slides.title: Answer back
slides.pivot: ask: what fact or example proves them wrong?
slides.followUp: cold call one board: is that proof, or just disagreeing?

items.text: Some people say a school garden is too much work. However, ___
items.answer: e.g. each class could look after it for one week, so the work is shared.
items.expect: a reason or example, not an insult

items.text: Some people say phones keep kids safe at school. However, ___
items.answer: e.g. the office can reach any parent in a minute.
items.expect: a reason or example, not an insult

items.text: Some people say a longer lunch means less learning. However, ___
items.answer: e.g. kids focus better in class after a proper break.
items.expect: a reason or example, not an insult

say: Finish each However with proof, so the other side has nothing left to say.
trap: writing No they're not, or That's dumb.
Fix: student asks what proves it, then rewrites with a fact or example.
notes.stretch: Add a This means sentence after your proof.
notes.help: Start with However, if... or However, most kids...
notes.prep: Guided practice on the answer back. Accept any fair reason or example. SC2.

slides.ask: How would you finish However with proof, not an insult?

slides.title: Mine: watch me finish strong
slides.extract: Twenty steps a day is no life for a polar bear. Bears need space, and they need the cold. Please stop bringing new polar bears to your zoo from this year.
highlights: Twenty steps a day is no life
Bears need space, and they need the cold
Please stop bringing new polar bears
slides.source: Model letter, written for this session

beats: POINT to Twenty steps.
SAY: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. My ending is where I sell it.
First I restate my position and echo my hook,
so the end joins up with the start.
POINT to space and cold.
SAY: Then I sum up my two reasons in one quick sentence.
ASK: Which part is my last sentence? Show me 1, 2 or 3.
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, voices off... show me.
EXPECT: 3 fingers
SAY: Last comes one clear thing the director can do, and when.
That's my call to action.
trap: ending with Thank you for reading.
Fix: student swaps it for Please, one action, and when.
notes.stretch: Rewrite my last line so it echoes the hook even more closely.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: That is why... Please... by...
notes.prep: Mine: the zoo letter's conclusion. Restate, sum up, call to action.

slides.title: Which part of the ending?
slides.pivot: ask: is it the position again, the reasons, or an ask?
slides.followUp: cold call one student: which words told you?

items.text: Please put twenty new bike racks near the front gate by Term 1.
Our school needs somewhere safe to leave our bikes.
More racks mean fewer stolen bikes and, most importantly, more kids riding.

say: Here's a new conclusion, chopped up and mixed.
Show me: 1 restate, 2 sum up, 3 call to action.
trap: calling the sum up a restate because both sound sure.
Fix: ask does it list the reasons? Then it's the sum up. Student re-shows.
notes.stretch: Say the three sentences in the right order.
notes.help: Look for Please first, because that's usually the call to action.
notes.prep: Guided labelling on a new issue, in mixed order. SC1.

slides.title: Which is the strongest call to action?
slides.prompt: A letter to the council about a dangerous crossing near school.

options.text: Thank you very much for reading my letter.
options.misconception: thinks being polite is the same as asking for action

options.text: Please put a crossing supervisor at our gate by Term 1.
Crossings near schools are very dangerous.
options.misconception: restates the problem but asks for nothing

notes.answer: B - one clear action, and when
beats: SAY: Think like the council. Which one tells you exactly what to do?
ASK: Which is the strongest call to action?
15 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then cold call a C: where could C go instead?
Less -> ask of each: could the council do this tomorrow? Re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: It's B. It asks for one thing, and it says when.
trap: choosing C because it sounds strong.
Fix: ask what does C ask the council to do? Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Decision point before drafting: can they tell an action from a restate or a thank you?

slides.title: Ours: let's finish the shade letter

rows: Some say hats are enough. However, ...
Shade keeps us sun safe and equipment cool.
Plant trees along the oval by next summer.

slides.prompt: You write the However and the restate. I scribe it.

notes.answer: e.g. However, hats only shade our faces.
beats: SAY: Let's finish ours. The sum up and call to action are planned.
You write the two hardest lines.
ASK: Write our However line. What proves hats aren't enough?
40 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: hats only shade faces
SCAN boards for proof, not an insult.
80%+ -> cold call two boards, class picks one.
Less -> point to our plan's Other side row, re-ask.
ASK: Now write our restate, echoing the hook we chose in Session 1.
40 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: one picture from our hook, plus our position
trap: a restate that copies the hook word for word.
Fix: student keeps one image and adds the position.
notes.stretch: Write a final question to end our letter.
notes.prep: Ours: the class letter is now complete. Read it aloud together before the You Do if time allows.

slides.title: Yours: answer back and finish strong
slides.task: Do the warm-up, plan your ending, write it in your writing book, then read your whole piece aloud.
slides.frame: Some people say ___. However, ___. Please ___ by ___.
slides.extendedTask: a short warm-up, the ending plan, then the answer back and conclusion drafted, completing the big piece

notes.answer: an answer back with proof and a three-part conclusion
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Three minutes on the warm-up.
Then plan your ending and write it, so your piece is finished today.
SAY: Let's read the steps together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
CONFERENCE first with anyone from yesterday's exit list.
ASK: Read your partner your hook, then your last line. Do they echo?
30 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 30 seconds. Go.
Eyes back in 3, 2, 1.
EXPECT: Yes, both talk about...
TIME 25 minutes: warm-up 3, plan 6, writing 13, read-aloud at 22.
trap: a call to action with no action, like I hope you agree.
Fix: student rewrites it as Please, one action, and when.
notes.stretch: three last lines, then fix your weakest sentence.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: circle the part, then a starter per line.
notes.prep: Yours: the last two paragraphs. Every student leaves with a full draft for Week 5 feedback. SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: The library should stay open at lunch. It gives quiet kids a safe place, builds reading and costs nothing extra.
Write the call to action that finishes this conclusion.

notes.answer: e.g. Please open the library every lunchtime from next week.
beats: SAY: Here's a new conclusion with the last line missing. Finish it.
ASK: Write the call to action that finishes this conclusion.
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: Please... one action... and when
RECORD who writes a restate or a thank you.
They start Week 5 with a conference.
trap: writing another reason instead of an action.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new conclusion. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Read your partner your hook and your last line. Do they echo each other?

notes.answer: open - the partner can hear the hook in the last line
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
ASK: How sure are you that your conclusion ends with a clear call to action?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
A thumb up with a wrong exit board matters most.
SAY: You've written a whole persuasive piece this week.
Next week you'll get feedback and make it even stronger.
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. The draft goes to Week 5 feedback. SC2.
